Hatchlings of the Atlantic bobtail squid Sepiola atlantica emerge from their fertilised eggs at a remarkably small size, with a dorsal mantle length at birth of just 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm]. This diminutive dimension places juveniles among the smallest of the sepiolid squids at the onset of the exotrophic transition, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises early independence from endogenous yolk reserves. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], the embryonic period, from syngamy to the emergence of the free-swimming larva, lasts approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days]. This relatively protracted incubation is consistent with the slow developmental rates observed in other cold-water cephalopods. Following hatching, the juvenile squids begin an extended period of somatic growth and active planktotrophic feeding, gradually transitioning through the post-metamorphic juvenile stage as they increase in body mass and mantle dimensions.

The protracted juvenile growth phase culminates in the attainment of sexual maturation, a milestone marked by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of functional reproductive organs. For Sepiola atlantica, the time since birth at puberty has been documented as 190 days [tp = 190 days] when individuals are reared at 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]. This is the age at which the dorsal mantle length at puberty reaches approximately 1.7 cm [Lp = approximately 1.7 cm], a dimension that represents a considerable fraction of the species' ultimate adult size. The transition is characterised by rapid gonad maturation and the development of the hectocotylus in males, a modified arm used for sperm transfer during copulation. This size threshold, coinciding with first mating behaviour, marks the entry into the reproductively active adult stage, after which individuals are considered sexually mature and capable of spawning. The concordance between the mantle length and the timing of reproduction is a common pattern in cephalopod life histories.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial given its modest terminal body size. Field records indicate that a female Sepiola atlantica can achieve a cumulative reproductive output at death of 161.0 eggs  when maintained throughout her life at 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]. This lifetime fecundity is generated through multiple spawning events, as females deposit eggs in small, gelatinous clutches attached to the substrate. Each reproductive event appears to yield a modest batch of eggs, with repeated spawnings occurring over the course of the adult phase. The total number of eggs produced is comparatively high for a sepiolid of this mantle length, suggesting an efficient allocation of somatic resources toward reproductive effort. The energetic cost of this intensive reproductive schedule is substantial, likely constrained by the finite availability of prey and the metabolic demands of egg production in a temperate environment.

The lifespan of Sepiola atlantica is relatively short, as is typical for many small-bodied coastal cephalopods that exhibit a single breeding season. In captivity at 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], the maximum longevity recorded is 270 days [am = 270 days], representing the total duration from hatching to natural mortality. This life span encompasses the entire post-embryonic trajectory: a juvenile phase of approximately six months dedicated to growth, followed by a brief but intense reproductive period of several weeks. The dorsal mantle length at death reaches a maximum of 2.1 cm [Li = 2.1 cm], a terminal size that is only about 0.4 cm larger than the length at puberty, indicating that significant somatic growth slows considerably after maturation. Instead, energy is heavily directed toward reproduction, culminating in physiological senescence and death shortly after the cessation of spawning.

Comparative analyses with other sepiolid squids reveal that the life-history traits of Sepiola atlantica are consistent with a fast-lived, capital-breeding strategy typical of small-bodied cephalopods in temperate shelf waters. The age at birth of 45 days [ab = 45 days] at 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C] is notably longer than that reported for some tropical species, likely reflecting a lower thermal optimum for embryonic development. The time since birth at puberty of 190 days [tp = 190 days] yields a relatively rapid transition to maturation compared to the total lifespan, leaving approximately 80 days for reproductive activity. at a temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]The cumulative reproductive output of 161.0 eggs  underscores a high per-capita fecundity for a squid whose adult mantle length reaches only 2.1 cm [Li = 2.1 cm] at a temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]. These demographic parameters highlight a tightly constrained life cycle in which rapid growth, early maturation, and a single, intensive spawning period are key adaptations to a seasonally productive environment.
